questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which scoring system uses clinical features and inflammatory markers to stratify the probability of appendicitis and reduce negative appendicectomy?
questions.concept: Low scores permit observation and high scores permit surgery without imaging, while intermediate scores are those in which ultrasound or computed tomography adds most value.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Acute Abdomen

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes small bowel from large bowel obstruction on a plain abdominal radiograph?
options: Central dilated loops with valvulae spanning the full width in small bowel, and peripheral loops with haustra not crossing the lumen in large bowel
Free gas under the diaphragm in small bowel obstruction
questions.concept: Recognising the level directs the search for the cause, since adhesions and hernia dominate small bowel obstruction while carcinoma, volvulus and diverticular disease dominate the large bowel.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Acute Abdomen

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which finding in a patient with adhesive small bowel obstruction indicates that conservative management should be abandoned?
options: Localised tenderness with fever, tachycardia, leucocytosis or a rising lactate suggesting strangulation
questions.concept: Most adhesive obstruction settles with drip and suck, so the skill lies in detecting the minority with compromised bowel before infarction occurs, and water-soluble contrast both predicts resolution and hastens it.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Acute Abdomen

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Why does a caecal volvulus require operative treatment whereas a sigmoid volvulus is usually first managed endoscopically?
options: The caecum cannot be reliably decompressed or fixed endoscopically, so resection or caecopexy is needed, while a flatus tube decompresses the sigmoid
Sigmoid volvulus cannot be reached endoscopically
questions.concept: Recurrence after sigmoid decompression is high, so elective sigmoid resection follows during the same admission in a fit patient.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Acute Abdomen

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which transfusion strategy is supported by evidence in a stable surgical patient without cardiac disease?
options: A restrictive threshold, transfusing at a haemoglobin around 7 to 8 g per dL
A liberal threshold of 10 g per dL
questions.concept: Restrictive strategies reduce exposure without worsening outcomes in most groups, and the decision should also consider symptoms and ongoing bleeding rather than a number alone.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Transfusion of Blood

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which complication is caused by transfusing large volumes of stored blood rapidly?
options: Hypothermia with hypocalcaemia from citrate, hyperkalaemia and a coagulopathy of dilution
questions.concept: Warming the blood, monitoring ionised calcium and giving components in balanced ratios in major haemorrhage address these problems, which is why massive transfusion protocols exist.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Transfusion of Blood

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which ratio of components is used in a major haemorrhage protocol for trauma?
options: Approximately equal units of red cells, plasma and platelets
Red cells alone until the haemoglobin is corrected
Crystalloid until 4 litres have been given
questions.concept: Damage control resuscitation combines balanced components with permissive hypotension, limited crystalloid, tranexamic acid and rapid haemorrhage control.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Transfusion of Blood

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which drug reduces mortality in a bleeding trauma patient if given within 3 hours of injury?
questions.concept: The CRASH-2 trial showed benefit that was lost and possibly reversed if given later, which is why the time window rather than the laboratory result determines the decision.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Transfusion of Blood

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which laboratory-guided approach reduces blood product use in major surgery?
options: Viscoelastic testing with thromboelastography or rotational thromboelastometry to target the specific defect
questions.concept: Because it distinguishes fibrinogen deficiency, platelet dysfunction and hyperfibrinolysis at the bedside, it allows targeted rather than blanket component therapy.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Transfusion of Blood

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Why does stored red cell transfusion not immediately improve tissue oxygen delivery as much as expected?
options: Depleted 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate shifts the dissociation curve left, so unloading is impaired until it is regenerated over hours
questions.concept: Reduced deformability and the accumulation of microparticles are the other components of the storage lesion, which is one argument for restrictive transfusion.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Transfusion of Blood

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which imaging modality is preferred for evaluating a discrete breast lump in a woman under 35?
options: Ultrasonography, because dense breast tissue limits mammographic sensitivity
questions.concept: Mammography becomes the primary modality after about 40 as the breast becomes fattier, and both are combined with clinical examination and needle biopsy in triple assessment.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Breast

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which axillary procedure has replaced routine clearance for a clinically node-negative breast cancer?
options: Sentinel lymph node biopsy using dye and radioisotope
questions.concept: It stages the axilla accurately with far less lymphoedema and shoulder morbidity, and further treatment of the axilla is then guided by the sentinel node result.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Breast

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which patient with breast cancer requires trastuzumab, and what must be monitored?
options: One whose tumour overexpresses HER2, with monitoring of left ventricular ejection fraction
One with an oestrogen-receptor-positive tumour only
questions.concept: Cardiotoxicity is usually reversible unlike that of anthracyclines, but the two are not given concurrently because the risk is additive.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Breast

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which factor makes breast-conserving surgery inappropriate and mandates mastectomy?
options: Multicentric disease, a large tumour relative to breast size, or inability to achieve clear margins
questions.concept: Because conservation with radiotherapy gives equivalent survival to mastectomy when margins are clear, the decision rests on achieving local control and an acceptable cosmetic result.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Breast

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which condition presents as a lump with skin tethering and a history of trauma or surgery, and can mimic carcinoma on imaging?
questions.concept: Because it can produce a hard irregular mass with microcalcification, biopsy is often required, and it should not be diagnosed on history alone.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Breast

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which endocrine treatment is appropriate for a premenopausal woman with an oestrogen-receptor-positive tumour?
options: Tamoxifen, with ovarian suppression added in higher-risk disease
questions.concept: Aromatase inhibitors are ineffective while the ovaries respond to rising gonadotropins, so they are used only with ovarian suppression or after the menopause.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Breast

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which presentation of breast cancer carries the worst prognosis and is treated with primary systemic therapy?
options: Inflammatory breast cancer with peau d'orange from dermal lymphatic involvement
questions.concept: It is a clinical diagnosis, it is understaged by imaging, and neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by surgery and radiotherapy is the standard sequence.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Breast

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Why does a BRCA1 mutation carrier require different surveillance and risk-reduction advice from a sporadic case?
options: The lifetime risk of breast and ovarian cancer is high and bilateral, so MRI surveillance and risk-reducing surgery are considered
questions.concept: BRCA1 tumours are typically triple negative and high grade, they respond to platinum agents and PARP inhibitors, and cascade testing of relatives follows identification.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Breast

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which formula estimates the fluid requirement in the first 24 hours after a major burn?
options: The Parkland formula, 4 mL per kg per percent burn of Ringer lactate, half in the first 8 hours
2 mL per kg per percent of colloid
10 mL per kg per percent of saline
questions.concept: The time is calculated from the moment of injury rather than from admission, and urine output of 0.5 to 1 mL per kg per hour is the practical guide to adequacy.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Burns

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which depth of burn is characterised by blistering with a moist pink painful base and brisk capillary refill?
options: Superficial partial thickness, which heals without grafting
questions.concept: Deep partial thickness burns are drier, mottled and less painful with sluggish refill, and full thickness burns are insensate, leathery and dry, requiring excision and grafting.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Burns

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which feature suggests inhalational injury and mandates early consideration of intubation?
options: Facial burns with singed nasal hair, soot in the oropharynx, hoarseness and stridor
Burn over 20 percent surface area alone
questions.concept: Airway oedema progresses over hours and makes later intubation extremely difficult, so a low threshold for early definitive airway control is the safest approach.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Burns

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which procedure relieves the respiratory or circulatory embarrassment of a circumferential full thickness burn?
questions.concept: Escharotomy addresses the constricting burnt skin whereas fasciotomy addresses raised compartment pressure, and the two are needed in different situations though they may be combined in high-voltage injury.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Burns

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which graft is used to cover a large full thickness burn where donor site is limited?
options: A meshed split thickness autograft, expanding the available donor skin
questions.concept: Split thickness grafts contract more and give poorer cosmesis than full thickness grafts, which are reserved for the face and hands where quality matters most.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Burns

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Why is albumin or colloid generally withheld in the first 8 to 12 hours after a major burn?
options: Capillary permeability is greatly increased so colloid leaks into the interstitium and worsens oedema
questions.concept: As permeability recovers after about 12 to 24 hours colloid becomes more useful, which is why some protocols introduce it in the second phase of resuscitation.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Burns

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which injury is diagnosed clinically and treated before any imaging?
options: Tension pneumothorax, treated by immediate needle or finger thoracostomy
questions.concept: Waiting for a radiograph in a hypotensive patient with absent breath sounds and distended neck veins risks cardiac arrest, so decompression precedes confirmation.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Thoracic Trauma

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which finding on chest drain output after insertion indicates the need for thoracotomy in haemothorax?
options: An immediate drainage of more than 1500 mL, or more than 200 mL per hour for 2 to 4 hours
questions.concept: These thresholds identify ongoing surgical bleeding from a systemic vessel or the heart, which will not stop with drainage alone.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Thoracic Trauma

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which chest injury produces paradoxical movement of a segment of the chest wall?
options: Flail chest from segmental fractures of three or more adjacent ribs
questions.concept: The underlying pulmonary contusion rather than the mechanical instability usually determines outcome, and management centres on analgesia, physiotherapy and ventilatory support with surgical fixation in selected cases.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Thoracic Trauma

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which injury should be suspected in a patient with blunt chest trauma, widened mediastinum and a fractured first rib?
options: Traumatic aortic injury, investigated by contrast computed tomography angiography
questions.concept: The commonest site is just distal to the left subclavian at the ligamentum arteriosum, and blood pressure and heart rate control precede definitive endovascular or open repair.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Thoracic Trauma

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which finding suggests tracheobronchial injury after blunt trauma?
options: A large persistent air leak with pneumomediastinum and failure of the lung to re-expand after drainage
questions.concept: Bronchoscopy confirms the site, and repair is usually required because a major airway disruption will not heal with drainage alone.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Thoracic Trauma

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Why does a patient with cardiac tamponade from penetrating trauma have a normal chest radiograph?
options: The acute pericardium does not distend, so a small volume raises pressure without enlarging the cardiac silhouette
questions.concept: This is why the diagnosis rests on clinical signs and focused ultrasound, and why pericardiocentesis of even 20 mL can be life-saving as a bridge to thoracotomy.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Thoracic Trauma

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which condition presents with severe pain on defaecation with bright bleeding and a sentinel pile at the posterior midline?
questions.concept: Internal sphincter hypertonia maintains the fissure, so treatment aims to relax it with a topical nitrate or calcium channel blocker, with botulinum toxin or lateral sphincterotomy for chronic cases.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Colon, Rectum and Anus

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which classification describes haemorrhoids that prolapse on straining and reduce spontaneously?
questions.concept: First degree bleed without prolapse, third degree require manual reduction and fourth degree are irreducible, and the grade guides the choice between banding, sclerotherapy and haemorrhoidectomy.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Colon, Rectum and Anus

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which finding indicates a fistula in ano rather than a simple perianal abscess?
options: A chronic discharging external opening with an internal opening in the anal canal
questions.concept: Goodsall's rule predicts the tract, though it is unreliable posteriorly, and magnetic resonance imaging is used for complex or recurrent fistulae, especially in Crohn disease.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Colon, Rectum and Anus

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which operation is appropriate for an obstructing carcinoma of the sigmoid colon in an unstable patient?
options: Hartmann procedure with resection, end colostomy and closure of the rectal stump
questions.concept: Avoiding an anastomosis in an unprepared, contaminated and physiologically compromised patient removes the risk of leak, with reversal considered later once the patient has recovered.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Colon, Rectum and Anus

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which margin determines whether a rectal cancer requires abdominoperineal resection rather than anterior resection?
options: Involvement of or proximity to the sphincter complex in a very low tumour
questions.concept: Total mesorectal excision with an adequate circumferential resection margin is the oncological principle in both operations, and neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy may permit sphincter preservation.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Colon, Rectum and Anus

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Why is a defunctioning stoma often created after a low anterior resection?
options: It does not prevent an anastomotic leak but reduces the septic consequences if one occurs
questions.concept: Because the low pelvic anastomosis has the highest leak rate and the most serious consequences, diversion is a damage-limitation measure rather than a preventive one.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Colon, Rectum and Anus

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Fluid, electrolyte & nutritional support in surgery
questions.stem: Which route of nutritional support is preferred whenever the gut is usable, and why?
options: Enteral, because it maintains mucosal integrity, reduces bacterial translocation and costs less with fewer complications
questions.concept: Even small trophic volumes preserve villous height and gut-associated lymphoid tissue, which is why the maxim if the gut works use it governs practice.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Metabolic Response to Injury and Nutritional Support

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Fluid, electrolyte & nutritional support in surgery
questions.stem: Which electrolyte abnormality should be anticipated when feeding is started in a severely malnourished surgical patient?
options: Hypophosphataemia with hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia of the refeeding syndrome
questions.concept: Insulin release drives these ions intracellularly for phosphorylation, so calories are increased gradually with thiamine and daily electrolyte monitoring in the first days.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Metabolic Response to Injury and Nutritional Support

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Fluid, electrolyte & nutritional support in surgery
questions.stem: Which fluid is inappropriate as the sole maintenance fluid in a postoperative adult, and why?
options: Five percent dextrose alone, because it provides no sodium and risks dilutional hyponatraemia
questions.concept: The postoperative state with raised vasopressin impairs free water excretion, so hypotonic fluid in excess is a recognised cause of avoidable hyponatraemia and cerebral oedema.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Metabolic Response to Injury and Nutritional Support

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Fluid, electrolyte & nutritional support in surgery
questions.stem: Which metabolic change characterises the catabolic ebb and flow phases of the response to major surgery?
options: An initial hypometabolic ebb phase followed by a hypermetabolic catabolic flow phase with negative nitrogen balance
questions.concept: Understanding the timing explains why aggressive feeding in the earliest phase is unhelpful and why enhanced recovery protocols aim to blunt the response with analgesia, early feeding and mobilisation.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Metabolic Response to Injury and Nutritional Support

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Fluid, electrolyte & nutritional support in surgery
questions.stem: Which complication is specific to central parenteral nutrition and requires vigilant prevention?
questions.concept: A dedicated lumen, strict aseptic handling and prompt removal when no longer needed reduce it, and metabolic complications include hyperglycaemia, hepatic steatosis and electrolyte disturbance.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Metabolic Response to Injury and Nutritional Support

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Fluid, electrolyte & nutritional support in surgery
questions.stem: Why does the classic starvation response differ from the response to sepsis or major injury?
options: In starvation ketone adaptation spares protein, whereas the cytokine-driven catabolism of injury continues to break down muscle despite feeding
questions.concept: This is why nutritional support in critical illness attenuates but cannot abolish loss of lean mass, and why control of the underlying insult remains the priority.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Metabolic Response to Injury and Nutritional Support
